1.note: The implied “you” in the imperative **Listen** is plural because Yahweh is addressing multiple people. The word “your” and the implied “you” in imperatives are plural in verses 1–2 and 4–7 for the same reason. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here Yahweh is speaking of people who earnestly try to live rightly as if they were **pursuers of righteousness** who chased after it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who earnestly try to live rightly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [pursuers of what is righteous]

1.q: צ֣וּר חֻצַּבְתֶּ֔ם וְ⁠אֶל מַקֶּ֥בֶת בּ֖וֹר נֻקַּרְתֶּֽם
1.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people’s ancestors as if they were a **rock** from which they had been **hewn** and a **pit** from which they had been **dug**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your ancestors, who are like a rock from which you were hewn and a hole from which you were dug]

1.q: צ֣וּר חֻצַּבְתֶּ֔ם וְ⁠אֶל מַקֶּ֥בֶת בּ֖וֹר נֻקַּרְתֶּֽם
1.note: This could mean: (1) that Yahweh is using both the **rock** and the quarry (the **pit**) that he describes to mean both Abraham and Sarah, whom he names in the next verse. The UST models one way to express this meaning. (2) that Yahweh is using the **rock** to represent Abraham and the **pit** to represent Sarah. The image would be of Sarah carrying Isaac, the ancestor of the Israelites, in her womb. Alternate translation: [you ancestor Abraham, who is like a rock from which you were hewn, and your ancestor Sarah, who is like a quarry from which you were dug, since she carried your ancestor Isaac in her womb]

The expression **you were hewn** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from which someone hewed you]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **hole** that is characterized by being a **pit**. The idea is that at a quarry, workers create a hole as they dig out rocks, and eventually it becomes a deep pit. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and to the deep pit]

The expression **you were dug** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [from which someone dug you]

2.note: Here, **father** represents “ancestor.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Abraham your ancestor]

Here, **she bore you** represents the fact that Sarah is the ancestress from whom the people are descended. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to Sarah, from whom you are descended]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The implication is that Yahweh called Abraham when he was still **one** person, before he had any children. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I called him when he was only one person]

Here, **made him many** represents making Abraham’s descendants many. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and gave him many descendants]

3.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

Here, **Zion** represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh will comfort the people of Zion; he will comfort]

Here, **all of her desolations** represents all the ruined places where no one lives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he will restore people to all of ruined places]

3.q: וַ⁠יָּ֤שֶׂם מִדְבָּרָ⁠הּ֙ כְּ⁠עֵ֔דֶן וְ⁠עַרְבָתָ֖⁠הּ כְּ⁠גַן יְהוָ֑ה
3.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **Eden** was fertile and beautiful, so **her wilderness** will become. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he will make her wilderness as fertile and beautiful as Eden and her desert plain as lush as the garden of Yahweh]

Isaiah is speaking of Zion as if it were a woman who could own a wilderness, which is why he calls it **her wilderness**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Zion’s wilderness]

The expression **will be found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Joy and gladness will fill her]

The terms **Joy** and **gladness** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Great joy]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Joy** and **gladness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [People rejoicing and being glad]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [thanksgiving and the voice of song will be found in her]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thanksgiving**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sound of people giving thanks]

Here, **the voice of song** represents the sound of people singing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the sound of singing]

4.q: הַקְשִׁ֤יבוּ אֵלַ⁠י֙ עַמִּ֔⁠י וּ⁠לְאוּמִּ֖⁠י אֵלַ֣⁠י הַאֲזִ֑ינוּ
4.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully to me, my people and my nation]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Do this because]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his **law** as if it were a person or thing that could **go out** and travel to the nations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will proclaim my law]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will make my just decisions available]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his justice as if it were **a light** that would guide the peoples to know what is right. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as a guide for the peoples]

5.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [How I make things right]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the time when he will act righteously as if it were **near** in space. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [My righteousness will soon be revealed]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way I save people]

Here Yahweh is speaking of his **salvation** as if it were a person or thing that could **go out** and travel to people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will save the peoples]

Here, **my arms** represents Yahweh’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and my power will judge the peoples]

For poetic purposes, Isaiah is using two different words that have basically the same meaning. The ULT translates each one as **wait** because English does not have two different words that it can use in this context. But if your language does, it would be appropriate to use them here.
See how you translated the term “coastlands” in 40:15. Alternate translation: [Everyone on earth]

Here, **my arm** represents Yahweh’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they will wait for me to act powerfully]

6.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of looking upward as if it were possible to physically **Lift up your eyes**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Direct your gaze]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Do this because]

The point of this comparison is that just as **smoke** vanishes and disappears, so **the heavens** will vanish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [the heavens will vanish and disappear, just as smoke vanishes]

The expression **will be dissipated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the heavens will dissipate]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a garment** wears out and falls apart, so **the earth** will wear out. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and the earth will wear out and fall apart just as a garment wears out and falls apart]

The point of this comparison is that just as the heavens and the earth will perish, so **its dwellers** will die in the same way. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and its dwellers will die in the same way, just as the heavens and earth perish]

There is another Hebrew word with the same consonants as the word that the ULT translates as **thus**. That other word means “gnat,” and some interpreters believe that it is intended here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [like a gnat]

Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the passing away of the heavens and the earth and the permanence of his salvation. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [In contrast to those things, my salvation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But the way I save people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and my saving righteously]

The expression **will not be dismayed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and nothing will ever dismay my righteousness]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [knowers of what is right]

Here Yahweh is speaking of people knowing and cherishing his **law** as if it were physically located **in their heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who cherish my law]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when men reproach you]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [human beings]

The expression **be dismayed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and do not let their revilings dismay you]

8.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

8.q: כַ⁠בֶּ֨גֶד֙ יֹאכְלֵ֣⁠ם עָ֔שׁ וְ⁠כַ⁠צֶּ֖מֶר יֹאכְלֵ֣⁠ם סָ֑ס
8.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the people who oppose his people as if they were a **garment** and **wool** that a **moth** and a **grub** would **devour**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who oppose you will be destroyed as easily as a moth devours a garment, and they will perish as easily as a grub devours wool]

The pronoun **them** refers to the people who reproach and revile God’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the moth will devour those who reproach you]

Yahweh uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the perishing of those who oppose his people and the permanence of his righteousness and salvation. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [however, my righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [but the way I do right]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and my salvation will be to the generation of generations]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and my saving of people]

Yahweh is using **to the generation of generations** as a common expression of the culture to mean “for all future ages” or “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all future ages]

9.q: עוּרִ֨י עוּרִ֤י לִבְשִׁי עֹז֙ זְר֣וֹעַ יְהוָ֔ה
9.note: Isaiah is speaking of the **arm of Yahweh** as if it were a living person who could **Awake** and **put on strength**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Begin to act powerfully, begin to act powerfully, Yahweh, with your mighty arm]

Isaiah is repeating forms of the verb **Awake** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Wake up completely]

Here Isaiah is speaking of becoming strong as if **strength** were clothing that one could **put on**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [become strong]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [put on your might and become strong]
Here, **arm** represents Yahweh’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [power of Yahweh]

9.q: הֲ⁠ל֥וֹא אַתְּ הִ֛יא הַ⁠מַּחְצֶ֥בֶת רַ֖הַב מְחוֹלֶ֥לֶת תַּנִּֽין
9.note: Isaiah is using the question form to affirm that it was indeed Yahweh’s arm that crushed Rahab and pierced the sea monster. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It was certainly you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the sea monster!]
Here, the word **you** is singular and refers to the **arm of Yahweh**, which is addressed as a single individual. Make sure this is clear in your translation.

The implication is that **Rahab** and **the sea monster** are names for a fearsome chaos monster that Yahweh defeated, an image that also represents Egypt, whom Yahweh conquered when he rescued his people. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the one having hewn Rahab the chaos monster in pieces, the one having pierced the sea monster, representing Egypt]

10.q: הֲ⁠ל֤וֹא אַתְּ־הִיא֙ הַ⁠מַּחֲרֶ֣בֶת יָ֔ם מֵ֖י תְּה֣וֹם רַבָּ֑ה הַ⁠שָּׂ֨מָה֙ מַֽעֲמַקֵּי־יָ֔ם דֶּ֖רֶךְ לַ⁠עֲבֹ֥ר גְּאוּלִֽים
10.note: Isaiah is using the question form to affirm that it was indeed Yahweh who dried up the sea and its deep waters. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It was indeed you, the one having dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass through!]

10.q: הַ⁠מַּחֲרֶ֣בֶת יָ֔ם מֵ֖י תְּה֣וֹם רַבָּ֑ה הַ⁠שָּׂ֨מָה֙ מַֽעֲמַקֵּי־יָ֔ם דֶּ֖רֶךְ לַ⁠עֲבֹ֥ר גְּאוּלִֽים
10.note: The implication is that this describes when Yahweh dried up the sea so that the people he had redeemed from Egypt could cross through it on dry ground. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the one having dried up the sea of Egypt, the waters of the great deep, he who made the depths of the sea a way on dry ground for the redeemed to pass through]

Even though Isaiah is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **he who made the depths of the sea** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [you who made the depths of the sea]

Isaiah is using the adjective **redeemed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the redeemed people]

11.note: Isaiah is using the adjective **ransomed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [And the people whom Yahweh ransomed]

Isaiah is using **their heads** to represent the whole persons of the returning people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and joy of eternity will be upon them]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **joy** that is characterized by **eternity**, that is, joy that lasts forever. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and everlasting joy]

11.q: שָׂשׂ֤וֹן וְ⁠שִׂמְחָה֙ יַשִּׂיג֔וּ⁠ן נָ֖סוּ יָג֥וֹן וַ⁠אֲנָחָֽה
11.note: Isaiah is speaking of **Gladness and joy** and of **sorrow and sighing** as if they were living things that could **overtake** people or **flee** from them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will become glad and joyful; they will no longer experience sorrow or sighing]

The terms **Gladness** and **joy** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Great gladness]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **Gladness** and **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Glad and joyful feelings]

The terms **sorrow** and **sighing** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [deep sorrow]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **sorrow** and **sighing**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being sad and grieving]

12.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I am he** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the importance of this declaration. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [It is I, Yahweh, who is he who comforts you]

The word **you** is feminine singular in these instances because it refers to Zion, the city of Jerusalem personified as a woman. The words “you” and “your” and the implied “you” in imperatives are feminine singular in verses 19–23 for the same reason. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction.

Verse 16 suggests that by **you**, Yahweh means Zion. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Who are you, Zion, that you should be afraid]

Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke his people for being afraid of mere mortals. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [have no reason to be afraid of your fellow man]

Here the masculine terms **man** and **son of man** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. See the UST.

The expression **is given up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he withers and dies]

The point of this comparison is that just as **grass** withers and dies quickly, so a mortal person will soon die. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [he is given up as quickly as grass withers and dies]

13.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of creating the sky as if he **stretched** it **out** like a tent, and of creating the earth as if he **founded** it like a building. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one having created the heavens and having established the earth]

13.q: חֲמַ֣ת הַ⁠מֵּצִ֔יק כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר כּוֹנֵ֖ן לְ⁠הַשְׁחִ֑ית וְ⁠אַיֵּ֖ה חֲמַ֥ת הַ⁠מֵּצִֽיק
13.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the oppressor’s fury as if it were **heat**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the fury of the oppressor as he prepares to destroy? But where is the fury of the oppressor]

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that the oppressor’s fury will come to nothing and no longer be a threat. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But the heat of the oppressor is nowhere to be found!]

14.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the captive being set free as if the prisoner were **opened**, like a door or chains being unlocked. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [hastens to be set free]

Here, **The stooping one** represents a prisoner who is bent down in captivity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [The bent-down prisoner]

The expression **to be opened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [for someone to release him]
Here, **the pit** represents captivity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in captivity]

Yahweh is using **his bread** to represent food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his food]

15.note: This expression has two possible meanings. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. This could mean: (1) the one who calms the see when it is in a turmoil. Alternate translation: [the one calming the sea when its waves roar] or (2) the one churning up the sea so that its wave surge. Alternate translation: [the one stirring up the sea so that its waves roar]

Here Yahweh is speaking of calming the stormy sea as if he made the **sea rest** the way a person rests. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one calming the sea when its waves roar]

Yahweh is using the possessive form **Yahweh of Armies** to describe himself as one who is characterized by commanding vast **Armies**, the hosts of heaven. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yahweh who commands the armies of heaven]

16.q: לִ⁠נְטֹ֤עַ שָׁמַ֨יִם֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠יסֹ֣ד אָ֔רֶץ וְ⁠לֵ⁠אמֹ֥ר לְ⁠צִיּ֖וֹן עַמִּ⁠י־אָֽתָּה
16.note: Here, the word **to** marks the phrases **to plant the heavens and to found the earth and to say to Zion, ‘You are my people’** as the goal or purpose of what Yahweh has done. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Here Yahweh is speaking of telling someone what to say as if he had physically **put** his **words in** the person’s **mouth**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I have told you what to say]

Here Yahweh is speaking of protecting someone as if he **covered** the person **with the shadow of** his **hand**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I have protected you with my power]

Here Yahweh is speaking of creating the sky and the earth as if he **plant**ed **the heavens** like a garden and **found**ed **the earth** like a building. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to create the heavens and to establish the earth]

Here, **Zion** represents the people who live there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and to say to the people of Zion, ‘You are my people’]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [that they are my people]

17.note: Isaiah is repeating forms of the verb **Awaken** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Awaken yourself! Yes, awaken yourself]
Here, the word **yourself** is singular because Isaiah is addressing the city of Jerusalem as a single individual. If your language marks number on pronouns and commands, use the singular form here.

Here, **Jerusalem** represents the people who live in the city. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Arise, people of Jerusalem]

17.q: שָׁתִ֛ית מִ⁠יַּ֥ד יְהוָ֖ה אֶת כּ֣וֹס חֲמָת֑⁠וֹ & שָׁתִ֖ית
17.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s anger and punishment as if it were a **cup** from which Jerusalem **drank**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [received from the hand of Yahweh the full measure of his anger; you experienced]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the punishment that made Jerusalem reel as if it were **the cup of staggering**, a cup of wine so strong that it caused people to stagger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the goblet that made you stagger]

Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe a **cup** that is specifically a **goblet** and that is characterized by causing **staggering**. The idea is that this goblet can hold so much wine that if someone drank everything in it when it was full, he would stagger drunkenly. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the goblet that holds enough wine to make a person stagger drunkenly]

Isaiah is using **you drained it** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Jerusalem experienced Yahweh’s punishment fully, down to the last drop. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you experienced all of it]

18.q: אֵין־מְנַהֵ֣ל לָ֔⁠הּ מִ⁠כָּל־בָּנִ֖ים יָלָ֑דָה וְ⁠אֵ֤ין מַחֲזִיק֙ בְּ⁠יָדָ֔⁠הּ מִ⁠כָּל־בָּנִ֖ים גִּדֵּֽלָה
18.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [There is no one guiding her from all of the sons she bore; indeed, there is no one holding her hand from all of the sons she raised]

Even though Isaiah has been addressing Jerusalem directly, here he speaks of her in the third person as **her**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the second person. Alternate translation: [There is no one guiding you]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both her sons and her daughters. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the children she bore … the children she raised]

Isaiah is speaking of the city of Jerusalem as if it were a mother who **bore** and **raised** her own **sons**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people who lived in her … the people who grew up in her]

19.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what the two disasters are together with the statement that they are meeting Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [These two disasters are meeting you: destruction and breaking, and famine and the sword; who will sympathize with you? Who will comfort you]

19.q: שְׁתַּ֤יִם הֵ֨נָּה֙ קֹֽרְאֹתַ֔יִ⁠ךְ מִ֖י יָנ֣וּד לָ֑⁠ךְ הַ⁠שֹּׁ֧ד וְ⁠הַ⁠שֶּׁ֛בֶר וְ⁠הָ⁠רָעָ֥ב וְ⁠הַ⁠חֶ֖רֶב מִ֥י אֲנַחֲמֵֽ⁠ךְ
19.note: The word **you** is feminine singular here because it refers to Jerusalem in verses 19-23. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [These two are meeting you, Jerusalem—who will sympathize with you?—destruction and breaking, and famine and the sword; who will comfort you, Jerusalem]

Isaiah is speaking of the two disasters as if they were living things that could come and **meet** Jerusalem. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [These two things have happened to you]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that there is no one to sympathize with or comfort Jerusalem in her disasters. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [no one will sympathize with you. … no one will comfort you.]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The first phrase states the general idea, and then the second phrase gives a specific example. Translate these phrases according to the decisions your team has made regarding translating parallelism in Hebrew poetry. Alternate translation: [who will sympathize with you, indeed, who will comfort you]

The terms **destruction** and **breaking** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [total destruction]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **destruction** and **breaking**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [being destroyed and broken]

Here, **the sword** represents war and violent death in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and famine and violent death in war]

Some ancient manuscripts read “who will I comfort you.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “who will comfort you.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [who will comfort you]

20.note: Here Isaiah is speaking of the people of Jerusalem fainting and collapsing as if they were **enwrapped**, wrapped up and overcome. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your sons have fainted]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both sons and daughters. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Your children]

The expression **are enwrapped** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [have fainted]

Isaiah says **at the head of all of the streets** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [at the head of the streets everywhere]

The point of this comparison is that just as **an antelope** caught **in a net** is helpless and unable to escape, so the people of Jerusalem lie helpless. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like an antelope caught in a net, helpless and unable to escape]

An **antelope** is a kind of swift-running wild animal that has horns. If your readers would not be familiar with what an antelope is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a wild animal]

Here Isaiah is speaking of the people experiencing Yahweh’s severe anger and punishment as if they were **full of the heat of Yahweh**, as though his wrath were something that filled them up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [being severely punished by the anger of Yahweh, the rebuke of your God]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **rebuke**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way your God rebukes them]

21.note: Isaiah is speaking of the people as if they were **drunken**, but he specifies immediately that this is not actually true by saying this is **not from wine**. He means that the people are dazed and staggering from their sufferings. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and dazed and staggering from your sufferings]

22.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **Thus says your Lord Yahweh** to introduce what follows as a direct quotation from Yahweh, spoken with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

22.q: לָקַ֛חְתִּי מִ⁠יָּדֵ֖⁠ךְ אֶת כּ֣וֹס הַ⁠תַּרְעֵלָ֑ה אֶת קֻבַּ֨עַת֙ כּ֣וֹס חֲמָתִ֔⁠י
22.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of ending his punishment of Jerusalem as if he had **taken from** her **hand the cup of staggering**, the cup of his anger that she had been drinking. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have taken from your hand the cup that made you stagger, the cup of my fierce anger]

23.note: Here, the word **that** marks **we may pass over** as the goal or purpose of the command **Lie prostrate**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [to make it possible for us to pass over]

Here Yahweh is speaking of punishing Jerusalem’s oppressors as if he would **put it**, the cup of his anger, **in the hand of the ones grieving** her for them to drink. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will make the ones grieving you drink of the cup of wrath]

Yahweh is using **your soul** to represent your whole self. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to you yourself]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [that you should lie prostrate so that they might pass over]

The point of this comparison is that just as people walk on **the earth** and **the street**, so Jerusalem’s enemies trampled over her, treating her body like ground to walk on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And you made your back into a surface for them to walk on, as if it were a road]
